reference.source: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: A skeletal dysplasia characterised by severe brachydactyly, short stature, and a hypoplastic mid-face with a small upturned nose
Two genetic forms are recognised: PRKAR1A variants (often with multiple hormone resistance) and PDE4D variants (frequently with more prominent intellectual disability and less hormone resistance)
Radiographs show short, broad tubular bones with cone-shaped epiphyses and premature epiphyseal maturation, overlapping the appearance of acromelic dysplasias
Both genes act in the cyclic-AMP/protein-kinase-A signalling cascade downstream of G-protein-coupled hormone receptors, linking the skeletal and endocrine features
Hormone resistance (to parathyroid hormone, and sometimes thyrotropin or gonadotropins) can resemble the biochemistry of pseudohypoparathyroidism
It is an important differential of Albright hereditary osteodystrophy, but GNAS is not the cause
Developmental delay is more typical of the PDE4D form
Management is supportive with orthopaedic care and endocrine management of any demonstrated hormone resistance
reference.pathophysiology: Acrodysostosis is a disorder of the cyclic-AMP/protein-kinase-A (PKA) signalling pathway. PRKAR1A encodes the type 1-alpha regulatory subunit of PKA, and PDE4D encodes a phosphodiesterase that degrades cyclic AMP; both regulate intracellular cyclic-AMP-dependent signalling downstream of G-protein-coupled receptors, including receptors for parathyroid hormone and other peptide hormones. Pathogenic variants perturb this signalling in chondrocytes and endocrine target tissues. In cartilage, disturbed PKA signalling accelerates epiphyseal maturation and impairs longitudinal bone growth, producing brachydactyly, cone-shaped epiphyses, and short stature. In hormone-responsive tissues, blunted signalling produces resistance to parathyroid hormone and sometimes other hormones, giving a biochemical picture that can overlap pseudohypoparathyroidism despite a normal GNAS gene.
additionalDifferentials: Other acromelic dysplasias (e.g. geleophysic and acromicric dysplasia)
additionalInvestigations: Skeletal survey demonstrating brachydactyly and cone-shaped epiphyses
Serum calcium, phosphate, and parathyroid hormone to assess PTH resistance
Thyroid function and other pituitary axis testing where resistance is suspected
Molecular genetic testing of PRKAR1A and PDE4D
Developmental assessment, particularly for the PDE4D form
redFlags: Symptomatic hypocalcaemia from significant PTH resistance
Airway or feeding compromise from severe mid-face hypoplasia in infancy
Spinal stenosis or neurological compromise from skeletal changes
reference.prognosis: Compatible with survival to adulthood; morbidity relates to short stature, hand deformity, variable hormone resistance, and, in the PDE4D form, cognitive impairment, rather than to a shortened lifespan.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing it as pseudohypoparathyroidism and missing the correct gene
Assuming all cases have hormone resistance, which is less prominent in the PDE4D form
Overlooking developmental delay as a clue to the PDE4D subtype
Failing to monitor calcium and PTH over time as resistance may evolve
references: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics
management: Treat hormone resistance as it emerges — active vitamin D (calcitriol) and calcium for parathyroid hormone resistance, and levothyroxine for thyrotropin resistance
Periodic endocrine surveillance of calcium, phosphate, parathyroid hormone and thyroid function
Orthopaedic and hand-surgery assessment for brachydactyly and skeletal deformity
Developmental and educational support, particularly in the PDE4D form associated with intellectual disability
Multidisciplinary care through clinical genetics, endocrinology and orthopaedics
Genetic counselling regarding PRKAR1A or PDE4D variants and their inheritance
